modules.name: Math
modules.header:
C's `<math.h>`: the elementary functions, in both the `double` and `float` forms C declares them in.
Bound rather than implemented, which is the point: a program that already links a C runtime and wants the same
answers its C code gets should ask the same library for them. `Rux/Math` computes these without a C runtime and
is the portable answer; this is here for interoperating with existing native code.
Two families are absent on purpose. `fabsf`, `frexpf`, `ldexpf` and `hypotf` are header inlines in the Universal
CRT rather than exported symbols, so declaring them would link on Unix and fail on Windows. The `nexttoward` pair
takes a `long double`, which is a different type on every target — 64 bits under the Universal CRT, an 80-bit
x87 value on x86-64 Unix, a 128-bit quad on AArch64 — so no one declaration is right everywhere.

modules.name: StdIo
modules.header:
C's stream I/O, declared against the C ABI types rather than against Rux's own widths.
A stream is a `*FILE` rather than a `*opaque`, so one handle cannot be passed where another was meant, and the two
position calls take a `*fpos_t` whose contents belong to the runtime. Sizes are `size_t` and returns are `c_int`,
which is what makes these declarations right on a target where those are not what Rux would have chosen.

modules.name: StdLib
modules.header:
C's `<stdlib.h>`: allocation, numeric conversion, sorting and searching, and process control.
Curated rather than complete. What is left out is left out on purpose, and the two groups worth naming are:
  - **Reach for the `strto*` family, not the `ato*` one.** `atoi` and its relatives cannot report failure: a string
    that is not a number and a string that says zero give the same answer, and a value too large is undefined
    rather than reported. `strtol` and its relatives report both, through an end pointer and through `errno`.
  - **`system` runs whatever the shell decides it means.** A command built from anything the program did not write
    itself is an injection, and what a "shell" is differs by platform. It is declared because a binding to C would
    be dishonest without it, not because it should be used.
`rand` is a pseudo-random generator with no guarantees at all: not the sequence, not the period, not the quality.
It must never seed a key, a token, or anything an adversary would like to predict; `Rux/Random` names its
generators and `Rux/Entropy` reaches the operating system.
`#Link` accepts only a constant declared in this file, so the selection is repeated per module rather than taken
from `C::CRuntime`, which names the same library and is what a reader should trust. Every module of this package
must name the same one: on Windows the Universal CRT and the legacy `msvcrt.dll` are separate runtimes with
separate state, and a stream opened by one is not a stream the other knows.

modules.name: String
modules.header:
C's `<char8[..].h>`: raw memory operations, and the byte-string operations that read until a terminator.
Two families live in one header for historical reasons, and they are not alike. The `mem*` calls take a length and
touch exactly that many bytes. The `str*` calls take no length and stop at the first zero byte, which means the
caller has promised there is one — and that promise, not the call, is what usually fails. Where both forms exist,
the counted one is the one to reach for.
Every declaration here names the exact symbol the C runtime exports, and is written against the C ABI types, so a
length is a `size_t` and a returned comparison is a `c_int`. Byte strings are `*char8` rather than `*c_char`: the
two are the same width, and `char8` is what a Rux string literal's `.data` already yields.
Nothing here is a safe interface, and none of it is what Rux code should reach for first — `Rux/Memory` and
`Rux/Text` do these jobs with lengths that are checked. This module exists to talk to C.
The notes below are plain comments rather than `///` documentation because an external block does not accept a doc
comment on its declarations, which is why every module of this package is written the same way.

modules.name: Time
modules.header:
C's `<time.h>`: the clocks, the calendar types, and the conversions between them.
Bound rather than implemented. `Rux/Time` is the calendar and clock interface to prefer — it has an epoch it
states, an error it reports, and no storage the next call may reuse — and this exists for interoperating with
existing native code that already speaks in `time_t` and `tm`.
Three of these calls return a pointer into storage the C runtime owns and the next call may overwrite:
`gmtime`, `localtime`, `asctime` and `ctime`. That is C's design and not something a binding can improve; copy
what you need before calling any of them again.

modules.name: Types
modules.header:
The C ABI's own types, spelled as the target's C environment spells them.
A declaration that has to match a C interface cannot be written in Rux's own widths: `int` is not `c_int` on every
target, and `long` is not one width at all. The aliases below say what each C type is on the target being built for,
so a binding is written once and stays right when the target changes. Nothing here has a run-time representation of
its own — each is exactly the Rux type it names.
The names follow C where C has one. `size_t`, `ptrdiff_t`, `intptr_t`, `uintptr_t`, `wchar_t` and `ssize_t` are the
spellings a C header uses, so a binding reads like the prototype it came from. The fundamental types have no typedef
to borrow, and their C spellings are Rux keywords, so those take a `c_` prefix: `c_int` for C's `int`.
The one thing that cannot be settled here is the signedness of `c_char`, which C leaves to the implementation. Every
currently supported target makes it signed, and that is what is declared; a binding that cares should say `c_schar`
or `c_uchar` rather than rely on it.

doc.summary: Finds the first byte equal to `ch` within the first `count` bytes.
doc.markdown:
Finds the first byte equal to `ch` within the first `count` bytes.
`ptr` is borrowed for the call and `count` bytes of it are read. `ch` is converted to an `unsigned char`
before comparison, so only its low eight bits matter. Returns a pointer into `ptr`, valid for as long as
`ptr` is, or null when no byte matches.
Runs in time proportional to `count` and allocates nothing.
`ptr` must be readable for `count` bytes. A `count` larger than the object reads past it.

params.name: ch
params.markdown: the character, as an `int` holding an `unsigned char` value or `EOF`

doc.returns: the address of the first matching byte, or null

items.name: memcmp
items.signature: pub extern func memcmp(lhs: *opaque, rhs: *opaque, count: size_t) -> c_int

doc.summary: Compares the first `count` bytes of two objects.
doc.markdown:
Compares the first `count` bytes of two objects.
Both are borrowed for the call. Returns a negative value when `lhs` orders first, zero when the two ranges
are identical, and a positive value otherwise; the magnitude means nothing. Bytes are compared as
`unsigned char`, so the result does not depend on whether plain `char` is signed.
Runs in time proportional to `count` and allocates nothing. Not constant-time: it stops at the first
difference, so it must not be used to compare secrets.
Both pointers must be readable for `count` bytes.
doc.returns: negative, zero or positive as the first differing byte orders

items.signature: pub extern func memcpy(dest: *var opaque, src: *opaque, count: size_t) -> *var opaque

doc.summary: Copies `count` bytes from `src` to `dest`.
doc.markdown:
Copies `count` bytes from `src` to `dest`.
`src` is borrowed and read; `dest` is borrowed and written. Returns `dest`. The two ranges must not overlap --
that is what `memmove` is for, and overlapping them here is undefined rather than merely unpredictable.
Runs in time proportional to `count` and allocates nothing.
`dest` must be writable for `count` bytes, `src` readable for `count`, and the two must not overlap.
doc.returns: `dest`

items.name: memmove
items.signature: pub extern func memmove(dest: *var opaque, src: *opaque, count: size_t) -> *var opaque

doc.summary: Copies `count` bytes from `src` to `dest`, correctly even when the two overlap.
doc.markdown:
Copies `count` bytes from `src` to `dest`, correctly even when the two overlap.
`src` is borrowed and read; `dest` is borrowed and written. Returns `dest`. Behaves as though the source were
copied to a temporary first, so sliding a range within one buffer works in either direction.
Runs in time proportional to `count` and allocates nothing.
`dest` must be writable for `count` bytes and `src` readable for `count`.
doc.returns: `dest`

doc.summary: Writes `ch` to each of the first `count` bytes of `dest`.
doc.markdown:
Writes `ch` to each of the first `count` bytes of `dest`.
`dest` is borrowed and written. `ch` is converted to an `unsigned char`, so only its low eight bits are
stored. Returns `dest`.
Runs in time proportional to `count` and allocates nothing.
`dest` must be writable for `count` bytes. This is not the call for clearing a secret: a compiler is entitled
to delete a write nothing reads back, and `Core::Zeroize` is the one that is not.

params.name: ch
params.markdown: the character, as an `int` holding an `unsigned char` value or `EOF`

doc.returns: `dest`

doc.summary: The length of a byte string, not counting its terminator.
doc.markdown:
The length of a byte string, not counting its terminator.
`str` is borrowed and read up to and including its first zero byte. Returns the count of bytes before it.
Runs in time proportional to the result and allocates nothing.
`str` must be non-null and must contain a zero byte. Without one this reads until it faults or wraps.
doc.returns: how many bytes precede the terminator

doc.summary: Compares two byte strings.
doc.markdown:
Compares two byte strings.
Both are borrowed and read to their terminators. Returns a negative value when `lhs` orders first, zero when
the two are equal, and a positive value otherwise. Bytes are compared as `unsigned char`.
Runs in time proportional to the shorter string and allocates nothing. Not constant-time.
Both must be non-null and terminated.
doc.returns: negative, zero or positive as the first differing byte orders

doc.summary: Compares at most `count` bytes of two byte strings.
doc.markdown:
Compares at most `count` bytes of two byte strings.
Both are borrowed. Stops at `count` bytes or at either terminator, whichever comes first. Returns the same
three-way answer `strcmp` does.
Runs in time proportional to `count` and allocates nothing. Not constant-time.
Both must be readable until a terminator or `count` bytes, whichever comes first.

params.name: count
params.markdown: how many bytes to compare at most

doc.returns: negative, zero or positive as the first differing byte orders

items.name: strcpy
items.signature: pub extern func strcpy(dest: *var char8, src: *char8) -> *var char8

doc.summary: Copies a byte string, terminator included.
doc.markdown:
Copies a byte string, terminator included.
`src` is borrowed and read to its terminator; `dest` is borrowed and written. Returns `dest`.
Runs in time proportional to the source length and allocates nothing.
`dest` must have room for the source's length plus one, which this call has no way to check and does not.
Getting that wrong is the classic buffer overrun; prefer `memcpy` with a length the caller computed.
doc.returns: `dest`

items.name: strncpy
items.signature: pub extern func strncpy(dest: *var char8, src: *char8, count: size_t) -> *var char8

doc.summary: Copies at most `count` bytes of a byte string, padding with zeros.
doc.markdown:
Copies at most `count` bytes of a byte string, padding with zeros.
`src` is borrowed; `dest` is borrowed and written. Returns `dest`. Writes exactly `count` bytes: shorter
sources are zero-padded to fill them.
Runs in time proportional to `count` and allocates nothing.
`dest` must be writable for `count` bytes. This does **not** terminate the result when the source is `count`
bytes or longer, which is the trap in its name: it is not a bounded `strcpy`.

params.name: count
params.markdown: how many bytes to write, terminator included

doc.returns: `dest`, which is not terminated when `src` filled the count

items.name: strcat
items.signature: pub extern func strcat(dest: *var char8, src: *char8) -> *var char8

doc.summary: Appends a byte string to the end of another.
doc.markdown:
Appends a byte string to the end of another.
`src` is borrowed; `dest` is borrowed, read to its terminator, and then written from there. Returns `dest`.
Runs in time proportional to the sum of the two lengths, since it finds the destination's end first.
`dest` must be terminated and must have room for both lengths plus one. Repeated appending is quadratic and
is a common accident: each call walks the destination from its start.
doc.returns: `dest`

items.name: strncat
items.signature: pub extern func strncat(dest: *var char8, src: *char8, count: size_t) -> *var char8

doc.summary: Appends at most `count` bytes of a byte string to the end of another.
doc.markdown:
Appends at most `count` bytes of a byte string to the end of another.
`src` is borrowed; `dest` is borrowed and written. Returns `dest`. Always terminates the result, so it writes
up to `count + 1` bytes past the destination's existing end.
Runs in time proportional to the destination's length plus `count`.
`dest` must be terminated and must have room for its own length plus `count` plus one. `count` bounds what is
taken from the source, not the size of the destination.

params.name: count
params.markdown: how many bytes to take from `src` at most

doc.returns: `dest`

rather than failing. Returns a pointer into `str`, or null when the byte does not occur.

items.name: strtok
items.signature: pub extern func strtok(str: *var char8, delimiters: *char8) -> *char8

doc.summary: Splits a byte string into tokens separated by any byte of `delimiters`.
doc.markdown:
Splits a byte string into tokens separated by any byte of `delimiters`.
`str` is borrowed and **modified**: a terminator is written over each delimiter found. Pass the string on the
first call and null on each call after it to continue the same scan. Returns the next token, or null when
none is left.
The scan's position is kept in storage shared by the whole program, so two interleaved scans destroy each
other and no two threads may use this at once. The string must be writable, which rules out a literal.

params.name: delimiters
params.markdown: the set of bytes that separate tokens

doc.returns: the next token, or null; the position is kept in storage shared by the whole program

doc.summary: C's `tm`: a calendar time broken into its components.
doc.markdown:
C's `tm`: a calendar time broken into its components.
Two of the fields are traps rather than conveniences, and both are C's rather than this binding's: `tm_year`
counts from 1900, so 2026 is 126, and `tm_mon` counts from zero, so December is 11. `tm_sec` reaches 60 for
a
leap second.
Declared once per system because the field order and the trailing members differ; the nine standard fields
are
the same everywhere and are all this declares.

doc.summary: Which of the package's C runtimes a call belongs to.
doc.markdown:
Which of the package's C runtimes a call belongs to.
On Windows this package spans two: `StdLib` and `Math` bind the Universal CRT, while `StdIo` and `Time` bind the
legacy runtime, because the Universal CRT does not export the formatted-output family. The two keep separate
`errno` storage, so reading one after a call into the other reports a value belonging to something else
entirely.
Everywhere else there is one runtime and both cases name it, so a caller that always passes the area matching
the module it called is right on all four systems and needs no target branch of its own.

cases.name: General
cases.doc: Where `C::StdLib` and `C::Math` are bound, and what plain `Errno` reads.

cases.name: Streams
cases.doc: Where `C::StdIo` and `C::Time` are bound. The same runtime as `General` except on Windows.

doc.summary: Whether the two areas are really two runtimes on this target.
doc.markdown:
Whether the two areas are really two runtimes on this target.
True on Windows and false everywhere else. A caller that passes the right area never needs to read this; it is
here so that a program can say why it is being careful, and so that a test can assert the split exists where it
is supposed to and does not where it is not.

doc.summary: The address of the calling thread's `errno`, in the runtime `area` names.
doc.markdown:
The address of the calling thread's `errno`, in the runtime `area` names.
Returns a pointer that runtime owns, valid for as long as the calling thread runs. Writing through it is how
C's `errno = 0` is spelled, which a caller does before a call whose failure is only reported through `errno`.
Pass the area matching the module whose call is being checked: `Streams` after anything from `C::StdIo` or
`C::Time`, `General` after anything from `C::StdLib` or `C::Math`. Passing the wrong one is not a compile error
and not a crash; it reads a different thread-local integer, which is the whole hazard this exists to remove.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
The address belongs to the calling thread and must not be handed to another one.
doc.returns: the address of that runtime's `errno` for this thread

doc.summary: The calling thread's current `errno` value, in the runtime `area` names.
doc.markdown:
The calling thread's current `errno` value, in the runtime `area` names.
Meaningful only after a call that documents setting it: no C function clears `errno` on success, so a value left
over from an earlier failure is still there. Clear it through `ErrnoLocationFor` before the call whose failure
is to be read.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: that runtime's `errno` for this thread

doc.summary: The address of the calling thread's `errno`, in the runtime `C::StdLib` and `C::Math` are bound to.
doc.markdown:
The address of the calling thread's `errno`, in the runtime `C::StdLib` and `C::Math` are bound to.
Exactly `ErrnoLocationFor(CRuntimeArea::General)`, and the spelling to use when the call being checked came from
one of those two modules. After a call from `C::StdIo` or `C::Time` on Windows this reads the wrong runtime's
storage, which is what `ErrnoLocationFor` exists to let a caller avoid.
Writing through it is how C's `errno = 0` is spelled, which a caller does before a call whose failure is only
reported through `errno`.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
The address belongs to the calling thread and must not be handed to another one.
doc.returns: the address of the general runtime's `errno` for this thread

doc.summary: The calling thread's current `errno` value.
doc.markdown:
The calling thread's current `errno` value.
Takes nothing and returns the value by copy. Meaningful only after a call that documents setting it: no C function
clears `errno` on success, so a value left over from an earlier failure is still there. Clear it with
`*ErrnoLocation() = 0` before the call whose failure is to be read.
On Windows this reads the Universal CRT's `errno`, which is the one `C::StdLib` and `C::Math` set. `C::StdIo` and
`C::Time` are still bound to the legacy `msvcrt.dll`, whose `errno` is a different variable in a different
runtime, so a failure reported by a call in either of those modules is not visible here. That split is a known
defect: the Universal CRT does not export the formatted-output family, so moving those modules across needs the
`__stdio_common_*` entry points declared first.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: the general runtime's `errno` for this thread
